newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Business urges SAfrica not to rush free trade deal.
newsitem.headline: Business urges SAfrica not to rush free trade deal.

text.p: Two key South African business federations on Monday urged the government not to rush into a free trade deal with the European Union (EU) cautioning that the continent's mandate was too harsh on vulnerable industries.
"We are concerned that it (the negotiating process) is being pushed at an indecently fast pace," said Philip Krawitz, the deputy president of the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob).

"We should not unduly delay the process but if speed is going to result in compromises for our economy, then Sacob's position is unequivocal: Pace it slowly," Krawitz told a joint meeting of parliament's trade and industry, agriculture and foreign affairs committees.

The South African government is preparing a negotiating mandate in response to tough instructions from the European Council earlier this year to its negotiators. Officials said on Monday this mandate would be ready by October 28.
Both Sacob and the Afrikaanse Handelsinstituut (AHI) called for the free trade agreement to be phased in over 15 years instead of the proposed 10 years, to allow a longer period of adjustment.

Business has tabled concerns that the EU's proposals could result in local products being rendered uncompetitive and lead to a loss of income of 2.45 billion rand for the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), comprising South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Lesotho and Swaziland.
The AHI proposed that the EU be called on to sponsor a regional development fund, administered by South Africa, to compensate SACU.
"It is suggested that the EU make available developmental funds to the customs union partners equal to the amount of lost revenue due to the free trade agreement," the AHI's Daan Botha said.
Department of Trade and Industry official Willem Bosman, disagreed with Sacob's position that the process was being rushed.
"This process is incestuous. We are debating amongst ourselves on hypothesis and unless we test it, we will be forever running around in circles -- We need to have a breakthrough now," Bosman said.
The EU has refused post-apartheid South Africa full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to its markets to developing countries in Africa, the Caribbean and Pacific.

Instead, the European Commission has handed South Africa a mandate which excludes up to 40 percent of its agricultural products, while calling on it to extensively reduce tariffs to ensure easier access to its market for European producers.
